title: The interior castle
hook: Teresa pictures the soul as a castle of many rooms, God at the center

segments.voice: Yesterday, The Imitation of Christ, and three Latin words: love to be unknown. Your line was follow quietly. Did you do something nobody saw? Day two hundred seventy-six.

A front hall gets all the traffic. The door opens and shuts, messages pile up, people come and go, and the little emergencies never stop. It's possible to spend years in the front hall of a life and never sit in the inner rooms. In 1577, a Spanish nun, sick and overworked, was told to write a book on prayer. She didn't know how to begin. Then, she said, a picture came to her. The soul is a castle. And many souls, she wrote, stay out in the courtyard. Today: the interior castle.
screen: `LIVING IN THE FRONT HALL.` → `A NUN WHO DIDN'T KNOW HOW TO BEGIN.` → `THE SOUL IS A CASTLE.`

segments.voice: Teresa of Ávila was a Carmelite nun in sixteenth-century Spain. She was funny, stubborn, practical and brave. She traveled rough roads by cart to found new convents, clashed with powerful people, and wrote books on prayer that are still read. In The Interior Castle, she asks us to picture the soul as a castle made of a single diamond or very clear crystal, with many rooms, the way Jesus said there are many dwelling places in his Father's house. In the King James Bible: "In my Father's house are many mansions." Teresa's rooms are arranged in seven sets, like rings, one inside another. And at the very center, in the innermost room, lives God, the King, shining through the whole crystal. Here's the surprise, in Teresa's telling. The castle is already there. God is already at the center. Nobody has to build anything. The task is to go in. And the door into the castle, she says, is prayer. The outer rooms are noisy. Things from outside creep in with you, she says, like snakes and vipers from the courtyard. That's normal. You keep walking. Further in, prayer grows quieter and simpler, and more is given than done. In the innermost rooms, Teresa describes a union with God she compares to rain falling into a river: you can't tell the waters apart anymore. But she's firm about one thing. The test of how far in you've gone isn't feelings. It's love of your neighbor, and humility.
screen: `A CASTLE OF CLEAR CRYSTAL.` · `GOD IN THE INNERMOST ROOM.` · `THE DOOR IS PRAYER.` · `THE TEST IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Picture a castle of clear crystal, light coming from its center. You're standing in a noisy outer room: your to-do list, your phone, today's worries crawling around. Don't chase them out. Just notice a door ahead of you. Walk through it, one room further in. It's a little quieter. Stay there. If you pray, you can simply turn toward the light at the center. The bell holds the time.
The interior castle. Teresa's picture of the soul: many rooms of clear crystal, with God living at the center.
Your line: there's a room further in. Today, when the front hall gets loud, take one breath and picture stepping through one more door. Day two hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Christians, especially Catholics and Carmelites, read Teresa's Interior Castle as a guide to growing in prayer, and use her picture of rooms moving inward to describe the life of prayer.

original.note: Spanish, in the Latin alphabet: the dwelling places, Teresa's own title for the book.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fairy-tale picture of a holy life.
what it means: God already lives at your center; prayer is the door, and the path goes room by room inward.
what a scholar hears: Las Moradas (1577), seven sets of dwelling places echoing John 14:2; and Teresa's insistence that the proof of prayer is love of neighbor.
